title: Hologram Heroes
intro: Each round shows a real problem. Pick the invention that solved it. Then meet the inventor, and a scientist working today.

levels.title: Two choices
levels.goal: Two rounds, two inventions to pick from.

levels.title: Three choices
levels.goal: Two rounds, three inventions to pick from.

levels.title: Four choices
levels.goal: Two rounds, four inventions. The problems are harder to spot.

inv_robot_arm.label: Unimate robot arm
inv_robot_arm.solved: The Unimate robot arm took over lifting and stacking hot metal parts in a factory.

inv_solar_still.label: Solar still
inv_solar_still.solved: The solar still uses sunlight to turn salt water into water that is safe to drink.

inv_electron_microscope.label: Electron microscope
inv_electron_microscope.solved: The electron microscope shows things too small for a light microscope to see.

inv_kevlar.label: Kevlar fiber
inv_kevlar.solved: Kevlar fiber is very strong for its weight, so ropes and boats can be strong and light.

inv_uv_camera.label: Far ultraviolet camera
inv_uv_camera.solved: The far ultraviolet camera took pictures of ultraviolet light from stars and gas in space.

inv_laserphaco.label: Laserphaco laser probe
inv_laserphaco.solved: Laserphaco is a laser tool for removing a cataract from the eye.

inv_foldscope.label: Foldscope paper microscope
inv_foldscope.solved: The Foldscope is a paper microscope that costs under $1 to make, so more people can have one.

inv_3d_printer.label: 3D printer (stereolithography)
inv_3d_printer.solved: This 3D printer turns a computer design into a solid part, one thin layer at a time.

inv_blue_led.label: Blue LED
inv_blue_led.solved: Bright blue LEDs made bright, energy-saving white LED light possible.

inv_sound_star.label: Space data turned into sound
inv_sound_star.solved: Sonification turns space data into sound, so people can study it by listening.

rounds.problem: Factory workers had to grab and stack hot metal parts all day.
People stranded at sea were surrounded by salt water, with nothing safe to drink.
Even the best light microscopes could not zoom in far enough to see the tiniest things.
Steel is strong but heavy. Ropes, boats and planes needed something strong and light.
Scientists wanted pictures of ultraviolet light from stars and gas in space. Our eyes cannot see this kind of light.
A cataract clouds the lens inside the eye. Eye surgeons wanted a more precise way to remove it.

devol.name: George Devol
bio: George Devol filed a patent for a robot arm in 1954.
In 1956 he and Joseph Engelberger founded Unimation. In 1961 the first Unimate arm went to work at a General Motors plant, where it followed programmed steps to stack hot metal parts.

telkes.name: Mária Telkes
bio: Mária Telkes was a scientist born in Budapest, Hungary, who came to the United States in 1925.
During World War II she developed a device that uses sunlight to make salt water safe to drink. It went into the military's emergency kits.

ruska.name: Ernst Ruska
bio: Ernst Ruska, born in Heidelberg, Germany, worked with Max Knoll to build the first electron microscope in 1931.
In 1933 Ruska built one that showed finer detail than a light microscope. In 1986 he shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.

kwolek.name: Stephanie Kwolek
bio: Stephanie Kwolek was a chemist at DuPont, born in New Kensington, Pennsylvania.
While looking for stronger, stiffer fibers, she discovered a new kind of material called a liquid crystalline polymer. It led to Kevlar, a fiber five times stronger than the same weight of steel.

carruthers.name: George Carruthers
bio: George Carruthers was born in Cincinnati and built his first telescopes by the time he was 10.
At the Naval Research Laboratory he led the team that built the far ultraviolet camera. In 1972, Apollo 16 astronauts set it up on the Moon.

bath.name: Patricia Bath
bio: Patricia Bath was an eye doctor. She finished her training as an eye doctor at New York University.
In 1981 she came up with Laserphaco, a laser tool and method for removing cataracts. She received a U.S. patent for it in 1988.

howard.name: Ayanna Howard
howard.why: Factory robot arms grew into robots that help people, including kids.
work: Co-founded Zyrobotics, which makes learning tech for children with special needs.
firstSteps: Started her career as a robotics researcher at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.
howard.yourStep: Write step-by-step directions for a simple task, like making a sandwich. Ask a friend to follow them exactly. Robots need directions that are just as clear.

nakamura.name: Shuji Nakamura
nakamura.why: Both made light and energy do useful work.
work: Professor at the University of California, Santa Barbara.
Shared the 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics with Isamu Akasaki and Hiroshi Amano for efficient blue LEDs. Their work made bright, energy-saving white light possible.
nakamura.yourStep: Look at a white light through the shiny side of an old CD. You may see that white light holds many colors.

prakash.name: Manu Prakash
prakash.why: The biggest microscope meets one made of paper.
work: Co-invented the Foldscope, a folded-paper microscope that costs under $1 to make. His co-inventors on its patent are James Cybulski and James Clements.
firstSteps: Earned degrees at the Indian Institute of Technology in India and at MIT.
prakash.yourStep: Put one drop of water on clear plastic wrap over a printed page. Look through the drop. It works like a tiny lens.

hull.name: Chuck Hull
hull.why: Both turned liquid chemicals into strong, solid things.
work: Invented stereolithography, one way to 3D print. UV light hardens liquid resin one thin layer at a time.
firstSteps: In 1983 his method made its first part, a small eye wash cup.
hull.yourStep: Build a small shape by stacking thin layers of paper or clay, one on top of the next. That is how a 3D printer builds things.

diaz_merced.name: Wanda Díaz-Merced
diaz_merced.why: Both study the sky with more than eyesight.
work: Turns space data into sound. This is called sonification.
Speaks widely about using sound to study space.
firstSteps: As a student, did an internship at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center. There she helped build early tools to study space data turned into sound.
diaz_merced.yourStep: Write down the temperature each hour for one day. Turn each number into a note: a higher number gets a higher note. Listen to your day.

ochoa.name: Ellen Ochoa
ochoa.why: Both used light to help people, and machines, see.
work: Co-inventor on three patents for optical systems, including ways for machines to recognize objects.
Flew in space four times and later directed NASA's Johnson Space Center.
firstSteps: Born in Los Angeles, California, in 1958.
In 1993 she became the first Hispanic woman in space.
ochoa.yourStep: Put a pencil in a clear glass of water and look from the side. The pencil seems to bend, because light changes direction when it goes from water to air.
